items.titleEn: Yesavage to throw off mound Friday as part of late-season comeback plan
bodyEn: CLEVELAND -- The Blue Jays need some heroes if they’re going to turn this forgettable season into one we remember, and Trey Yesavage is on the way.

Early in August, Yesavage underwent left knee surgery to repair his meniscus, but he’s scheduled to throw off a mound for the first time Friday at the Blue Jays’ complex in Dunedin, Fla. The 23-year-old has just over three weeks to get back by the end of the regular season, and in an AL Wild Card race that could be decided by a single game, that could make all the difference.
From here, this is what Yesavage’s ideal plan looks like:

1. The first bullpen -- When Yesavage throws off a mound Friday, the key will be how his knee responds the next day. This is Yesavage’s landing leg down the mound, so how will that respond to pitching closer to max effort?

2. Another bullpen -- If the first one goes well, the Blue Jays will need to see another. This one would likely come a few days later and could include a few more pitches, but will prove that Yesavage is ready to face hitters.
3. Live hitters -- This would likely be Yesavage facing some hitters down at the Blue Jays’ complex, close to max effort while simulating an inning or two.

4. Game action -- Keep in mind that the Triple-A Buffalo Bisons play their final game on Sept. 20. If Yesavage isn’t ready for this step by then, it could take the shape of a more formalized “sim game” at the complex, but he’s got a shot to line it up. Manager John Schneider says Yesavage would need “at least a game” to prove that he’s ready.
“If that goes well,” Schneider said, “we’ll see if he can help us out in some capacity.”

This schedule represents a perfect world for Toronto, but it’s what the club is hoping for. It’s difficult to put anything past Yesavage, either, who’s determined to get back if at all possible for another postseason run. If the Blue Jays fall out of this race by then, they are likelier to exercise extreme caution and back Yesavage off. But it looks like this will go down to the wire in late September.

Don’t expect Yesavage out there for six innings and 100 pitches, though. Instead, Toronto would be happy to see him build back up closer to half of his usual workload. Perhaps that lands him around three innings, four if he’s ultra efficient. The club is chasing his sheer upside at this point, not a grind-it-out start.

“That would make it interesting for a bullpen-y bulk day, with him being part of it,” Schneider said. “That would be nice. It just depends on how much time he’s missed, how much he can build up. Is it an inning or two? Is it three or four? We’ll cross that bridge when we get there.”

Schneider added that, if Yesavage comes back, it would be more tempting to just start Yesavage in the first inning, not using an opener, then figure out the bullpen from there. Most bulk relievers are pitchers caught between starting and relieving, but Yesavage would invent the “super bulk” role for the stretch run if this all works out, capable of filling a few innings with legitimately dominant upside.
So much still needs to go right between now and then, but Yesavage has a chance, and all the Blue Jays need is a chance.

items.titleEn: Cease's durability continues to define his dominant year
bodyEn: CLEVELAND -- Dylan Cease is an overachiever. Somehow, after signing the biggest free-agent contract in the history of the Toronto Blue Jays, he’s exceeding expectations.

One year in, we’re already holding Cease’s 2026 season up against Cy Young winners of the past, from Roy Halladay’s peak seasons to Robbie Ray’s dominance in ‘21 and those two years of Roger Clemens, which live in a quiet corner of Blue Jays history but may never be topped.

That’s the ground Cease already stands on. If he’d given the Blue Jays an ERA just over 3.00 with some “wow” moments throughout the year, that would have been deemed a complete and total success, but he’s unlocked another level of himself. With six more scoreless innings in the Blue Jays' 11-0 victory Wednesday night in Cleveland, the biggest win of the Blue Jays’ season, Cease now owns a 2.25 ERA over 156 1/3 innings. He’s a workhorse starter with closer stuff. He’s a hitter’s nightmare who sticks around for the sixth and seventh innings.
That durability is the dividing line between good and great. Baseball is littered with hard throwers who stall out at 4 2/3 innings, but Cease has some old-school to him.

“I have a really good process,” Cease said. “I’m going from start to start and making little adjustments, then discussing with the group what I need to work on and where I can get better. I like my ability to execute right now, and even when I’m not at my sharpest, I can command my fastball enough to get outs. I like where I’m at.”
What’s a “process,” though? That word is intentionally mysterious.

In José Berríos’ peak seasons with the Blue Jays, which were built upon durability, we came to know the persona of “La Makina.” He was always working out, always lifting, always pushing his body to the limit. Cease, on the other hand, seems so much more laid-back. It almost tricks you into believing that this all comes naturally to him.

“It’s different, but it’s really consistent,” manager John Schneider said. “His throw days are consistent, his lift days are consistent and he does a lot of stuff behind the scenes in the weight room. You see it a little bit in his bullpen when he’s got his belts on, the stuff, the gadgets. He’s got a lot going on. He’s very meticulous with it, but not like the workout guru that José is.”
This is where Cease’s old-school approach to pitching meets the new age. Those gadgets, as Schneider calls them, may look a little odd at times, but they seem to be working.
“He’s very aware of all of that stuff. What’s Tom Brady’s thing, pliability?” Schneider said. “He’s very pliable. Dylan’s very aware of that stuff.”

Cease has topped 100 pitches in 16 of his 26 starts this season, which leads the Majors. Sure, part of that is the Tom Brady magic and some of it is a natural gift, but it’s also a mindset. Cease believes, fully and truly, that it’s his job to go seven-plus innings each time out. The bullpen is there to close out the game, not share the load with him equally.

This was new for Schneider and pitching coach Pete Walker, too, hearing Cease walk in the morning of a start -- or breeze by them between the third and fourth inning -- and grunt “I’ve got 120 in me today.” Who’s going to question him?

“He’s been doing this for a while, and he’s been durable for a while, so he has a good feel for it,” Schneider said. “I don’t want to just call him a liar out of the chute, either. I want him to prove himself right -- and he has, a lot of the time.”
Whether the hardware ultimately lands with Cease or the Yankees’ Cam Schlittler, this season is Cy Young caliber. That can’t be wasted, which has too often happened to this franchise.

From Pat Hentgen (1996) to Clemens (‘97-’98), Halladay (‘03) and Ray (‘21), the Blue Jays have never made the postseason in a year their pitcher has won the Cy Young Award. It takes more than just one star pitcher to achieve the ultimate goal, of course, but it’s a cruel coincidence.

Cease can win you a Wild Card game if you get him there. Get him to an ALCS or World Series, and he’s talented enough to steal you two. That still feels far away for these Blue Jays, but without Cease, it wouldn’t even be a conversation.

items.titleEn: Ranking the 10 most impactful Trade Deadline moves, one month later
bodyEn: We all know who was the best player moved before this season's Trade Deadline. But now that we are one month clear of that date, has that player been the best midseason addition of the bunch?
Hint: No.
Tarik Skubal has been plenty good for the Dodgers, and you will find him in our ranking below of the top Deadline moves. But he's not No. 1. He's actually behind multiple other starting pitchers.
Here's a look at the top 10 most impactful Trade Deadline additions.
Notes: Limit one player per team. All stats updated through Tuesday unless noted otherwise.

1. Tyler Mahle, SP, BravesThe Braves were a Skubal suitor, but like every other club, they had to pivot after the jewel of the Deadline class was shipped to Los Angeles. Atlanta landed on the 31-year-old Mahle, who had a 5.13 ERA across 18 starts with the Giants and missed about a month of action earlier in the year due to a hamstring strain. Once the Deadline passed, he didn't even make it onto our list of the top 25 trades, but he has been everything the Braves could have wanted for their injury-ravaged rotation.

Mahle has allowed a total of five earned runs through his first five starts with the NL East leaders, spanning 30 1/3 innings. A greater reliance on his splitter has juiced Mahle's strikeout numbers and helped solve his issues against right-handed batters. His strikeout-minus-walk rate, which was a pedestrian 12.9% before the trade, is 23.1% since. And same-handed hitters have seen their OPS versus Mahle plummet from .848 to .583.

2. Clay Holmes, SP, CubsIn terms of total value, there is no doubt that the deal that brought Holmes to Chicago's North Side was the best one of Deadline season. Not only because he has been stellar for the Cubs, but because that swap with the Mets also included outfielder Tyrone Taylor, who owns a hefty .413/.462/.565 slash line through 52 plate appearances with Chicago.

Holmes hadn't pitched in about 10 weeks due to a fractured right leg when he was dealt to the Cubs. He stumbled a bit in his team debut, allowing four earned runs over four innings against the Royals on Aug. 8. But in four starts since then, he has given up one run in 25 innings.

3. Liam Hicks, C, RaysRays catchers finished 28th in wRC+ in 2024 and '25. They had been better this season ahead of the Deadline, but an offensive upgrade was still one of the club's top priorities. Enter Hicks, who perfectly fits the Rays' contact-heavy approach at the plate. But he's been doing a lot more than just putting the bat on the ball. He has been doing serious damage for the team with the best record in the American League.

Hicks, who has a .374 career slugging percentage through four Minor League seasons and had a .432 slug with the Marlins this year, is slugging .522 in 80 plate appearances with Tampa Bay. His .328 average, .425 on-base percentage and 163 wRC+ each rank inside the top 15 among the 195 hitters who have at least 80 PAs since Hicks first played for the Rays on Aug. 4.

4. Tarik Skubal, SP, DodgersHere's where Skubal slots in, and for just about any other pitcher, we'd be raving about his results with the Dodgers: a 3.00 ERA and an 11.1 K/9 rate over 30 innings (five starts). But for a reigning two-time Cy Young Award winner, Skubal's results draw more of a polite round of applause than a standing ovation. Still, he's looked really good his past few times out, including an 11-strikeout showing against the Pirates on Aug. 22. Skubal's FIP with the Dodgers is an impressive 2.29. That's third-best among qualified pitchers since August, trailing only the Rays' Drew Rasmussen (2.12) and the Reds' Chase Burns (2.17).

5. Luis García Jr., INF, YankeesIn no particular order, the Yankees' Trade Deadline priorities included bullpen help, a right-handed-hitting outfielder, another catcher and/or someone who could slot in at shortstop or third base.

And so, the Yanks' first headline add before the Deadline was ... a lefty-hitting infielder who plays on the right side of second base. However, García was still a huge get for a lineup that needed some pop. The 26-year-old has provided that, highlighted by a .511 slugging percentage, five home runs and 10 extra-base hits in his first 25 games with New York. He has multiple hits in four of his past eight games, including a four-hit night versus Houston on Aug. 25.
'Maybe the chain has power': Garcia's bat roaring with Yanks

6. Jo Adell, OF, GuardiansAcquiring left-hander Foster Griffin has been a plus for Cleveland, which can line him up behind the likes of ace Gavin Williams and standout rookie Parker Messick to form what could be a great rotation in a short playoff series. But what the Guardians really needed at the Deadline was more offensive firepower. Adell has brought that as he's posted 11 extra-base hits and an .815 OPS through 24 games.

Adell has been even better of late, slashing .327/.383/.527 over his previous 14 games. He enjoyed a six-RBI game in the middle of that stretch, something only one other Guardian (Angel Martínez) had achieved in the previous three calendar years. Prior to Adell's arrival, Cleveland ranked 27th in wRC+ (92). Since his first game on Aug. 4, they are tied for 11th in that stat (103).

7. Brett Bateman, OF, Blue JaysWhen the Blue Jays made the tough decision to trade away Kevin Gausman, they might have received their center fielder of the future in return. Bateman, Toronto's No. 16 prospect, made his MLB debut five days after the trade and has hit .317 with a .367 on-base percentage across 92 plate appearances since.

Speed and defense are considered his top tools, and those have definitely shown up in The Show. Bateman is 3-for-3 in steals through 20 games and has already racked up +3 outs above average during his short time in center.

8. Erik Miller, RP, Red SoxThe Red Sox made a huge splash on Deadline Day, grabbing catcher Adley Rutschman from the Orioles for five players, including three prospects. That deal hasn't yet worked out as Boston had hoped, but another move the club made on Aug. 3 has paid dividends. Miller, acquired from the Giants for former top prospect Marcelo Mayer, has absolutely dominated in a setup role in front of Aroldis Chapman, striking out 20 of the 46 batters he has faced. The lefty had thrown 10 1/3 scoreless innings before permitting a run during Monday's win over the Mariners. Most encouraging is the fact that Miller has walked only three batters in his 11 1/3 frames with Boston. He walked 22 batters in 32 2/3 innings with San Francisco before the trade.

9. Robbie Ray, SP, PadresSpeaking of walks, Ray has issued 16 in 26 1/3 innings with San Diego. But he has been able to work out of trouble often, as he has a 3.42 ERA through five starts. Ray indicated after his Aug. 18 start against the Mets that he has worked with Padres coaches to iron out some issues with his delivery, and when you include that evening's effort, the lefty has permitted only four earned runs through his past three outings (17 1/3 innings).

Ray has cut back on his four-seam fastball in favor of more changeups with the Padres. His usage on that pitch has increased 10 percentage points, up to 27%, and hitters have a .115 average (3-for-26) and a .448 OPS against it since he joined the NL Wild Card contenders.

10. Connor Norby, INF, RockiesNorby may be the only player in this top 10 who is not on a club with postseason hopes in 2026, but he is still worthy of inclusion after he reached base in each of his first 15 games with the Rockies after being acquired from the Marlins. The 26-year-old infielder has a .342 on-base percentage and seven extra-base hits through his first 21 games with Colorado. That includes Wednesday's walk-off victory over the Orioles, who drafted Norby in the second round in 2021.

He was once a high-ranking prospect in Baltimore's system but compiled an 89 wRC+ from 2024-26 with the Orioles and Marlins. Perhaps Norby will unlock his full potential while playing half of his games at the hitters haven that is Coors Field.

items.titleEn: Vladdy, Cease have Blue Jays looking their best in shutout win
bodyEn: CLEVELAND -- Wednesday night felt like one long exhale at Progressive Field for the Blue Jays. For a few hours, everything went right.

Sure, the Guardians helped the Blue Jays along by extending some innings with ugly defensive play, but all you’ll remember is the 11-0 win and Vladimir Guerrero Jr. finally looking like himself, if only for a night.
The win moves the Blue Jays back within 1 1/2 games of the Guardians for the final AL Wild Card spot, leapfrogging the Orioles and Rangers, who both lost Wednesday.
This is what mattered most:
1. Glimpses of the old Vladimir Guerrero Jr.

Oh, what a night. Guerrero’s three-run shot was the star of the show, but on either side of that, Vladdy ripped an RBI double off the wall in left and shot an RBI single the other way to add on another run in the sixth.

"I think he was ready to hit a curveball and he hit a curveball,” said Guardians starter Joey Cantillo. “The second at-bat, same thing. He was ready to hit a curveball and he hit a curveball. We got him the third at-bat, which is good. But he's a good hitter, so when you leave pitches over the plate, he's going to hit."

It’s been so long since one of these games. Guerrero, at his best, can hold a game in the palm of his hand and control it completely, but we haven’t seen that since the Blue Jays’ 2025 postseason run. After the home run and later the RBI single, there were chants of “Vladdy” coming down from the Blue Jays fans in attendance, something else we haven’t heard in too long.
2. Same old Dylan Cease
No one deserved an easy night at the office more than Dylan Cease, who’s been stuck pitching in low-scoring deadlocks all season long.

“That’s nice because it definitely allows for a little more margin of error,” Cease said. “Ultimately, I try to pitch the same way, which is not to give up runs, obviously. Maybe it changes some pitch selections here and there, but ultimately, I still want to pitch pretty similarly.”

He still did the same old thing, though, cruising through the Guardians’ lineup over six innings of scoreless ball with four strikeouts. The outing dropped his ERA to 2.25, and in the AL Cy Young race against the Yankees’ Cam Schlittler, every start is going to matter down the stretch.

Cease has become a lock for six-plus innings. It’s such a rare combination in the modern game, when so many younger pitchers chase strikeouts but can’t match that with the durability and deep starts. Cease does both, and does it about as well as anyone.

“Dylan's been a really good strikeout pitcher his entire career. I think adding the changeup... He used to be just north-south -- heaters at the top, and then the two spin pitches underneath. And now he's pitching," Guardians manager Stephen Vogt said.
"You add pitching to that arsenal and that stuff, you're going to get what you're seeing. He's been dominant this year. He's been one of the best, if not the best, starters.”
The bonus? Cease did this on 83 pitches. The Blue Jays need him out there as often as possible down the stretch, and this sets it up beautifully.
“That helps. I’m assuming I’m going to be going [every] five [days] for a while, so any chance to do something like that strategically, it’s a good idea,” Cease said.
3. A playoff mentality

Once you’ve been through what the Blue Jays went through in 2025, right up to Game 7 of the World Series against the Dodgers, “stress” takes on a different definition. In theory, a race for the third Wild Card spot should be much more manageable.
All of the “extras” can’t possibly compare, because there’s not the same media circus filling every empty second of manager John Schneider’s day, but there’s a mindset they can still reach back for.

“The mentality, going back to that Seattle series [in the ALCS] when we were coming home down 3-2,” Schneider said, “we just had to win tomorrow. We had to win the next day and figure it out. That’s the mentality right now.”

After Game 5 in Seattle, Ernie Clement sat at his locker, calm and cool, and said the Blue Jays were right where they wanted to be, controlling their own destiny even if they were down in the series. That’s the same mentality they need to carry through the final 22 games.

items.titleEn: Could this swing mark the return of vintage Vladdy?
bodyEn: CLEVELAND -- Months ago, in the early days of Vladimir Guerrero Jr.’s season-long struggles, he said he wouldn’t feel like he’s truly “back” until he could stand at home plate and watch his own home run fly. Only then could he really feel it.
The moment Guerrero made contact Wednesday night in Cleveland, he didn’t move an inch.

The towering, three-run shot soared to right field, a no-doubter from the moment Guerrero made contact. He strolled across the plate, in awe of what he’d done, and flipped his bat to the ground as the ball crashed into the bleachers. He hadn’t even left the dirt yet, hadn’t taken a single step down the first-base line.
Chants of “Vladdy! Vladdy! Vladdy!” rained down from the Blue Jays fans who had packed the bleachers above the Blue Jays’ dugout.

This is what it’s supposed to look like, and this is what we’ve spent all season waiting to see. On his first at-bat of the game, Guerrero made an excellent adjustment and drove a breaking ball off the left-field wall for an RBI double. Then, on the home run swing, his body exploded through the ball, the dozens of moving pieces finally coming together to play the right notes at the right time. We haven’t heard that song in ages.

This is only Guerrero’s eighth home run of the season, and he still doesn’t have one at Rogers Centre, but any flicker of hope is worth grabbing onto at this point. The Blue Jays are chasing the third AL Wild Card spot, which has been dancing just out of their grasp for too long, but Guerrero is the shortcut. Without Guerrero, the Blue Jays need to play their best baseball of the season in every possible way for the next three-plus weeks. If Guerrero suddenly comes back to life, though, that’s a rocket strapped to this ball team’s back.

At the same time, the Blue Jays -- and their fans, who have watched with frustration all summer -- have learned to be wary of false hope. Guerrero, his manager and his teammates have repeatedly said that when it comes, it will click in an instant and Guerrero will catch fire. His first seven home runs this season didn’t turn a spark into a flame, though, so why will this one?

All the Blue Jays have is the hope that it will, but that’s enough for now. The player that lit the 2025 postseason on fire hasn’t gone anywhere and certainly hasn’t disappeared, Guerrero has just been completely unable to find that version of himself in 2026. If he can find that again, or even a sliver of that player, it can help fuel a postseason run that would completely change how we view Guerrero’s 2026 season.
One more time we’re left to wonder: What if this is the swing? What if Vladdy’s found it?

items.titleEn: Each team's hottest pitching prospect right now
bodyEn: Last week, we identified the hottest hitting prospects in each organization. This week, we shift our focus to the top-performing pitchers during August from each farm system.

Diamondbacks right-hander David Hagaman struck out 48 in 31 1/3 innings, more whiffs than any Minor League pitcher has recorded in a calendar month this season. He's joined on our list below by five Top 100 prospects: Mariners righty Ryan Sloan (No. 8), Braves left-hander Cam Caminiti (No. 43), Cardinals southpaw Liam Doyle (No. 44), Angels righty Tyler Bremner (No. 46) and Athletics left-hander Jamie Arnold (No. 57).
Jump to: AL East | AL Central | AL West | NL East | NL Central | NL West
AMERICAN LEAGUE EAST

Blue Jays: Danny Thompson Jr., RHP (No. 15)Signed for $5,000 out of UNC Greensboro as an eighth-rounder last year, the 24-year-old right-hander posted a 2.95 ERA with 25 strikeouts over four outings (21 1/3 innings) with Double-A New Hampshire in August and strung together three straight quality starts from Aug. 1-14. His 93-96 mph fastball has gotten whiffs in the Eastern League (with aid from his lower release height), and he shows both a harder and sweepier breaking ball to keep hitters off-balance. His upper-80s changeup has been a more effective pitch since his move from High-A in June.

Orioles: Boston Bateman, LHP (No. 11)The Orioles suddenly find themselves flush with left-handers, including Bateman, who was part of the package received from the Padres in exchange for Ryan O'Hearn and Ramon Laureano at the 2025 Trade Deadline. He gets a lot of horizontal action on all of his pitches, highlighted by a mid-90s fastball and tight upper-80s slider. He didn't allow a run in 15 August innings in High-A while fanning 25 and limiting opponents to a .173 average.

Rays: Ty Johnson, RHP (No. 10)Tampa Bay moved Johnson to the Triple-A Durham bullpen in late July with an eye toward using him as a Major League relief option, and he’s certainly doing all he can to push for that debut in The Show. The 6-foot-6 righty struck out 19 of his 36 batters faced in August (52.8 percent) and allowed only one earned run on two hits and two walks over 11 ⅓ innings in that time. His 92-95 mph four-seamer and 85-87 mph slider both had whiff rates above 53 percent last month, so it’s clear his two-pitch approach can not only work but dominate in the shorter appearances.

Red Sox: Dylan Brown, LHP (No. 19)A 2025 eighth-rounder from Old Dominion, Brown ranks second in the Minors in strikeout rate (32 percent) during his pro debut thanks mainly to his command and deception with his four-seam fastball, which has added 2 mph this year but still averages 92 mph and tops out at 95. He permitted one earned run or less in four of his five starts last month in High-A, compiling a 2.66 ERA, .186 opponent average and a 31/4 K/BB ratio in 23 2/3 innings.

Yankees: Brendan Beck, RHP (No. 28)Beck quietly is enjoying one of the best pitching seasons in the Minors, ranking fourth in WHIP (1.05), fifth in ERA (2.75) and eighth in opponent average (.205). The 2021 second-rounder from Stanford can break out six different pitches but works primarily with a low-90s fastball with good carry and a tight low-80s slider. He made three Triple-A starts in August, posting a 1.62 ERA with 27 strikeouts in 16 2/3 innings before working a scoreless frame in relief for the Yankees.
AMERICAN LEAGUE CENTRAL

Guardians: Caden Favors, LHP (No. 29)The Guardians selected Favors in the sixth round out of Wichita State in 2024 because of his capacity to spin the ball, which translates into good carry on his low-90s fastball and plenty of action on his upper-70s curveball and upper-80s cutter. He gradually has acclimated to Double-A this season and logged a 2.54 ERA, .198 opponent average and 34/5 K/BB ratio in 28 1/3 innings last month.

Royals: Hunter Owen, LHP (unranked on Royals Top 30)A fourth-round pick out of Vanderbilt in 2023, Owen is a former member of Kansas City’s Top 30 prospects ranking, and he’s pushing himself back into prominence with a late charge at Double-A Northwest Arkansas. His 45 strikeouts over 27 innings were second-most in the Minors in August, and he racked up those K’s while posting a 1.33 ERA, .181 average-against and 1.19 WHIP over five starts. The 6-foot-5 southpaw hasn’t been big on velocity with a fastball only around 91-93 mph but managed to get whiffs across his four-pitch mix.

Tigers: Ben Jacobs, LHP (No. 7)After a promotion in late April, Jacobs had a 6.25 ERA through his first 10 starts with High-A West Michigan, though he had struck out 55 over 36 innings in that span. His numbers have been more dominant across the board recently with a 0.44 ERA, 25 strikeouts and .119 average-against over four August starts (20 2/3 innings) with the Whitecaps. The 22-year-old left-hander – who has three potentially above-average pitches in his fastball, slider and changeup – has a Midwest League ERA now at 4.08, and his 34.4 percent strikeout rate on the season ranks sixth among Minor Leaguers with at least 80 frames in 2026.

Twins: Adrian Bohorquez, RHP (No. 18)A forearm strain in mid-April put Bohorquez's season on hold for two months, but he rebounded to permit just one earned run in four starts between High-A and Double-A in August, while recording a .134 opponent average and 24/7 K/BB ratio in 20 innings. Signed for just $10,000 out of Venezuela in 2023, he relies heavily on a lively mid-90s four-seam fastball and a tight upper-80s slider.

White Sox: David Sandlin, RHP (No. 11)The White Sox need pitching help if they're going to stay atop the AL Central, and they could give Sandlin another look after he fashioned a 2.00 ERA with 19 strikeouts in 18 Triple-A innings last month. Part of the Jordan Hicks trade with the Red Sox in February, he has gone 2-1 with a 6.93 ERA during three short stints in Chicago this year. He succeeds when he can command his mid-90s fastball, and he complements it with an upper-80s cutter and a mid-80s sweeper.
AMERICAN LEAGUE WEST

Angels: Tyler Bremner, RHP (No. 2/MLB No. 46)The second overall pick in the 2025 Draft out of UC Santa Barbara, Bremner was slowed by illness early in his pro debut but returned to form in August with a 3.60 ERA, .196 opponent average and a 34/8 K/BB ratio in 25 innings between High-A and Double-A. His high-spin mid-80s changeup grades among the best in the Minors and he sets it up with a mid-90s fastball with plenty of carry and horizontal action.

Astros: Jagger Beck, RHP (No. 27)A rare nondrafted free agent signed out of high school, Beck turned pro for $150,000 in 2024 and missed most of last year with shoulder issues before emerging as one of the Astros' top young pitching prospects this summer. He owns two of the best breaking balls in the system, pairing an 82-85 mph slider with horizontal and vertical action with an 80-82 mph curveball, while his fastball sits in the low 90s. His 3.15 ERA in August actually was his highest since April, and he limited opponents to a .194 average while fanning 25 in 20 innings in Single-A.

Athletics: Jamie Arnold, LHP (No. 3/MLB No. 57)Coming off the best month of his pro debut (1.57 ERA, .200 opponent average, 29/6 K/BB ratio in 23 Double-A innings), Arnold started September with five scoreless frames in his first Triple-A start. The 11th overall pick in the 2025 Draft out of Florida State, he has a wipeout mid-80s slider that plays well off a 92-94 mph fastball that tops out at 97 with significant horizontal life in the opposite direction.

Mariners: Ryan Sloan, RHP (No. 2/MLB No. 8)Sloan yielded one run or less in four of his five August starts in Double-A, compiling a 2.84 ERA with 34 strikeouts and just two walks in 25 1/3 innings. Few pitchers can match his combination of stuff and strikes, as evidenced by his career 7.1 K/BB ratio -- the best in the Minors among pitchers with at least 150 innings in the last two seasons. The 2024 second-rounder from an Illinois high school gets outs with four different pitches: a four-seam fastball that averages 97 mph and reaches 100, a mid-80s sweeper, a sinker with similar velo to his four-seamer and a low-90s changeup with very little spin.

Rangers: Dalton Pence, LHP (No. 10)A star reliever in college at North Carolina, Pence has thrived as a starter since turning pro as a 2024 11th-rounder and currently ranks third in the Minors in ERA (2.59) and opponent average (.208). He moved to Triple-A in August and had no trouble adapting, posting a 2.19 ERA, .209 opponent average and 18 strikeouts in 24 2/3 innings. His low-90s fastball with carry and command plays as a solid offering, as do his sweeping slider and splitter/changeup, both of which sit in the low 80s.
Subscribe to the MLB Pipeline Newsletter
NATIONAL LEAGUE EAST

Braves: Cam Caminiti, LHP (No. 2/MLB No. 43)Caminiti was still technically a teenager when he made his Double-A Columbus debut on Aug. 6 (for two more days anyways), but he’s taken very well to the Minors’ second-highest level. Since that first outing with the Clingstones, the 6-foot-2 lefty owns a 2.13 ERA with 28 strikeouts over his first five Double-A starts (25 1/3 innings). Caminiti’s most effective pitch has been his sweeping breaking ball that has generated both whiff and chase.

Marlins: Jacob Kisting, RHP (No. 21)Dealt from the Twins to the Rays last November for Eric Orze and then to the Marlins in a package for Liam Hicks last month, Kisting leads the Minors in ERA (1.63) and stands second in opponent average (.184) and WHIP (0.90). Promoted to Double-A after the second trade, he responded with a 1.42 ERA and 24/6 K/BB ratio in 19 innings. How is the 2024 14th-rounder from Bradley doing this? He works from a low release height that adds deception, his low-90s fastball stands out with its horizontal action and his ability to command it, and he keeps batters off balance with two variations of a low-80s changeup.

Mets: Jonah Tong, RHP (No. 5)Tong’s tinkering to find a more diverse pitch mix has led to, well, mixed results at Triple-A Syracuse this season, but he found a groove in August and heads into September with a 0.84 ERA over his last four starts. He struck out 23 batters over 21 1/3 innings in that time, and after allowing just one hit over seven frames against Lehigh Valley on Saturday, he’s held batters to a .151 average in that span too. After being so fastball-changeup dominant in ‘25, Tong threw his cutter, curveball or slider 36.2 percent of the time during this four-start run that could earn him a shot back in the Majors before 2026 is out.

Nationals: Miguel Sime Jr., RHP (No. 10)Walks have been a constant theme of Sime’s first Minor League season, and that’s been no different of late with 12 free passes over his last four starts (14 1/3 innings). However, the 6-foot-4 righty is checking about every other box as a 19-year-old at High-A with a 1.26 ERA and .160 average-against in those four outings with Wilmington. He fanned 26 of his 62 batters faced (41.9 percent) in August and leads Nationals Minor Leaguers with 130 over 72 1/3 innings on the season as a whole. Sime’s high-octane fastball remains the headliner, but he can get empty swings with a slider, curveball and changeup too.

Phillies: Mavis Graves, LHP (No. 27)The 2022 sixth-rounder is Rule 5-eligible this offseason, and it is perhaps with that in mind that the Phillies moved him to the bullpen when they promoted him to Double-A Reading in late July. It’s been an effective move so far with the 6-foot-6 southpaw not allowing an earned run in any of his nine relief appearances in August. He fanned 18 batters and walked seven over 11 2/3 innings in that time. Graves has thrown his 79-81 mph slider 52 percent of the time, per Synergy, since his transition to the bullpen, and it’s easy to see why with a 56 percent whiff rate.
NATIONAL LEAGUE CENTRAL

Brewers: Josh Knoth, RHP (No. 9)Knoth hasn’t just returned from Tommy John surgery in an admirable fashion; he’s also picking up steam as 2026 progresses. The 21-year-old righty, who missed all of the 2025 season, had a 2.60 ERA with 26 strikeouts in his final five starts (27 2/3 innings) with High-A Wisconsin and earned his first promotion to Double-A Biloxi this week. (He allowed four earned runs in five frames during his debut Tuesday night.) Knoth throws everything with a ton of spin, including a riding four-seamer, and he’s established himself as one of Milwaukee’s most promising arms now that he’s healthy.

Cardinals: Liam Doyle, LHP (No. 2/MLB No. 44)St. Louis has always preached that it would be a process with the 2025 fifth overall pick, and we’re seeing many of the fruits of that process now at Double-A Springfield. Doyle owned a 1.31 ERA with 29 strikeouts and nine walks in 20 2/3 innings across four starts in August. His Aug. 13 outing against Northwest Arkansas marked the first time he completed six innings in an outing as a pro. Doyle’s 95-97 mph fastball remains the star of the show, and his upper-80s splitter is still his best secondary as he works on establishing breaking options.

Cubs: Jostin Florentino, RHP (No. 22)Florentino's delivery metrics (exceptionally low release height, good extension) are much more notable than his pure stuff (highlighted by a 90-mph fastball and 75-mph slider). Yet he continues to get outs and is coming off his best month of the season, logging a 2.95 ERA with a 22/5 K/BB ratio in 18 1/3 innings in High-A. He doesn't have a high ceiling but already has exceeded expectations since signing for $10,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2023.

Pirates: Thomas Harrington, RHP (unranked on Pirates Top 30)Harrington made his MLB debut last year with three appearances but has been back with Triple-A Indianapolis for all of 2026, bouncing between starting and bullpen roles. He’s moved back into bulk outings in August and the actual rotation on Aug. 13 with solid results: a 3.15 ERA, 1.25 WHIP and 17 strikeouts in his last four starts (20 innings). The 25-year-old righty uses a six-pitch mix (four-seamer, sinker, cutter, splitter, curveball, sweeper) to keep hitters guessing, and in this recent run, he has not thrown any individual pitch more than 25 percent of the time.

Reds: Mason Morris, RHP (No. 25)A former reliever at Ole Miss, the 2025 third-rounder has taken some time to find his rhythm in a larger role in his first full season but looked like he was clicking with a 3.31 ERA over his final four starts (21 1/3 innings) with Single-A Daytona. Morris was promoted to High-A Dayton and continued to be solid with one earned run allowed on two hits and two walks over 5 2/3 frames in his Midwest League debut last Saturday. Morris shows all three variations of a fastball but relies most on his 88-90 mph cutter.
NATIONAL LEAGUE WEST

D-backs: David Hagaman, RHP (No. 4)Acquired from the Rangers a year ago as part of the Merrill Kelly Deadline deal, Hagaman is hitting his stride in the D-backs organization now that he’s at Double-A. The 23-year-old led the Minors in strikeouts in August with 48 over 31 1/3 innings, and he fanned exactly 10 in three of his six outings during the month. He finished August with a 2.30 ERA and 1.18 WHIP. Hagaman – who has multiple weapons with above-average potential in his fastball, curveball and slider – is up to a career high 96 1/3 innings on the season as a whole and could be an offseason Top 100 contender given the quality of stuff and results in ‘26.

Dodgers: Cam Leiter, RHP (No. 16)Leiter is seeking to become the fifth member of his family to pitch in the Majors, following uncles Al and Mark and cousins Jack and Mark Jr. The Dodgers are handling him carefully after shoulder issues plagued him at Florida State, but he was utterly dominant in August with a 0.63 ERA, .104 opponent average and 23 strikeouts in 14 1/3 innings at two Class A levels. The 2025 second-rounder owns a pair of fastballs that sit at 97 mph and max out at 100, as well as a pair of quality breaking pitches in an 86-88 mph slider and a 78-82 mph curveball.

Giants: Jacob Bresnahan, LHP (No. 9)After winning pitcher of the year awards in 2024 (Rookie-level Arizona Complex League) and 2025 (Single-A California League), Bresnahan now ranks among the Minor League leaders in opponent average (.186, third), ERA (3.04, sixth), WHIP (1.08, ninth) and strikeout rate (30 percent). Acquired from the Guardians in exchange for Alex Cobb in 2024, he recorded a 3.33 ERA, .182 opponent average and 33 strikeouts in 27 innings last month between Double-A and Triple-A. His best pitches are a mid-80s kick change with nasty depth and a 92-97 mph fastball with some of the best carry in the Minors.

Padres: Lan-Hong Su, RHP (No. 9)Su signed with the Padres for $775,000 out of Taiwan last October, and it’s been a slow build for the 19-year-old ever since. After opening the season in the Arizona Complex League, he allowed 12 earned runs over 7 2/3 innings in his first three starts with Single-A Lake Elsinore from June 29 to July 9. Since then, he’s allowed only six earned runs total over his last seven starts, and in August specifically, he had a 3.55 ERA with 20 strikeouts and only three walks over four outings (12 2/3 innings). Known for his pair of breakers as an amateur, Su has found nice success with an upper-80s splitter of late in the California League.

Rockies: Mason Adams, RHP (No. 20)The Rockies picked up Adams from the White Sox at the Deadline for Brenton Doyle, and it hasn’t taken him long to make a good impression. Adams had a 2.08 ERA and 0.92 WHIP with 13 strikeouts and only three walks in his first three starts in the system with Triple-A Albuquerque, and that was enough for Colorado to push him to the Majors for the first time. The control artist has found modest success over two starts in the bigs through his six-pitch mix and should keep getting looks the rest of the way, provided he stays healthy after missing 2025 due to Tommy John surgery. He’s at 71 innings for the season across all levels.

items.titleEn: 'A tough draw': Blue Jays befuddled by Williams' career night in Cleveland
bodyEn: CLEVELAND -- For the Blue Jays to score another run against Gavin Williams, we might have been here all night.

This lineup facing that talent was a bad match for the Blue Jays, who lost 6-1 to the Guardians to open their biggest series of the season. The loss drops them to 2 1/2 games back of the Guardians in the AL Wild Card race and ties their season series, 2-2.
This is what mattered most:
1. Offense can’t handle Gavin Williams

September is no time to be tipping caps. Sure, Williams was absolutely dominant Tuesday night and struck out a career-high 13 -- possibly the best pitching performance the Blue Jays have seen this season -- but this team needs to find a way with the clock ticking. Even the lone run they scraped across was the result of two Guardians miscues following Kazuma Okamoto’s single in the fifth inning.

"Man, he was on,” manager John Schneider said. “That's 99-100 mph, two-seamer and four-seamer, breaking ball and sweeper. He was good. That's just a tough draw tonight through seven. A lot of swing-and-miss. He's got good stuff, but when you put command on it, too, there's outings like that."

This is where the lack of power is so clearly felt. Good luck trying to string together five base hits against Williams, but a bloop and a blast? Maybe that’s more doable, it’s just not something the Blue Jays are doing enough of.

The Blue Jays weren’t hitting Williams’ mistakes, either. Vladimir Guerrero Jr. got a couple of pitches over the plate, including a heater in the top of the sixth that we’ve seen him crush before, but popped a harmless fly ball into shallow right.

“You’ve got to get a guy or two on and you’ve got to clip one,” Schneider said. “To really string three, four, five hits together in a row, you’ve really got to time it up perfectly. That’s a tough draw tonight. You’ve got to get someone on and you’ve got to hit a mistake, he just didn’t make many of them tonight.”
2. Spencer Miles is the story of 2026
Don’t let any of this become “normal.” What Spencer Miles has done this season as a Rule 5 pick with just 14 2/3 innings of experience in the lower Minors is downright baffling.
This is supposed to be the point of the season where Miles hits a wall. Whether it be workload or just the league catching up to him, this incredible season has to fade eventually, right?

No chance. Miles just keeps getting better, a testament to both his talent and the meticulous plan he and the Blue Jays have nailed. Working as the opener Tuesday, Miles touched 100.2 mph with his sinker, a new career high as he dropped his ERA to 2.88 over 84 1/3 innings.
“It was hot and humid, and I’m like a rubber band out there, a little more elastic,” Miles said. “It’s that mixed with a day off. I felt good out there. I was letting it rip.”
Schneider is running out of ways to describe it at this point.

“I view him as one of our most trusted relievers, then you can still do something like this with him,” Schneider said. “We’re kind of flying in the dark in terms of things to compare him to. I remember going back to Spring Training like, ‘Is this kid going to make it?’ To go from that to where he is right now has been phenomenal.”

Next spring, get ready for the starter conversation with Miles. If he ends this season by creeping past 90 innings, that sets him up well for 2027, even if he’d still need to be managed throughout the season.
3. Who is Spencer Arrighetti in September?

Arrighetti gave the Blue Jays 3 2/3 innings of two-run ball on 62 pitches, the damage coming on Patrick Bailey’s two-run shot. This was a step back in workload, though, after he threw 79 pitches his last time out.

“We’re kind of at an imperfect spot to build up over the next three or four start days or bulk days, if you will,” Schneider said. “As much as we can, we’ll build him up and try to build off of last time. At the same time, we’ll try to take advantage of some guys we have here, too.”
At this point, it’s possible that Arrighetti stays in this role the rest of the way, with the Blue Jays using one or two “openers” in front of him.

items.titleEn: Perry makes 2026 All-Breakout Prospect Team
bodyEn: This story was excerpted from MLB Pipeline's newsletter. Subscribe to get it regularly in your inbox.

There are prospects who are obviously geared up for great seasons. No one should be surprised that Kevin McGonigle and JJ Wetherholt are starring in the big leagues, or that Dodgers outfielder Josue De Paula and Mariners left-hander Kade Anderson have dominated in the Minors.
Then there are prospects who seem to come out of nowhere. We recognize them annually with our All-Breakout team, the first edition of which in 2023 included Junior Caminero and Jacob Misiorowski.

Selecting from a pool of players that includes anyone who didn't crack the top 10 on our organization Top 30 rankings to start the year, I could have assembled an entire All-Breakout squad of current and recent Top 100 prospects. But I also wanted to reward some players who made the largest leaps.

Both pitchers on the All-Breakout team, Caden Hunter (Orioles) and Nolan Perry (Blue Jays), have gone from being unranked on org Top 30s to the Top 100 this year. They're joined by fellow Top 100 prospects Cooper Flemming (Rays), Murf Gray (Pirates) and Eric Hartman (Braves), and three more players who didn't make Top 30s in the preseason: Émilien Pitre (Mets), Franklin Primera (Red Sox) and Josiah Ragsdale (Cardinals).

Franklin Primera, C, Red SoxA $10,000 steal out of Venezuela in 2024, Primera has emerged as one of the best young catching prospects in the game. After tearing up the Rookie-level Florida Complex League with a .427/.549/.718 batting line in his first month playing in the United States, he has continued to rake in Single-A at age 19. He features advanced framing skills and possesses solid arm strength as well.

Taitn Gray, 1B, RaysOne of the best prep power prospects in the 2025 Draft, Gray hasn't disappointed since the Rays grabbed the Iowa product in the third round. He's hitting .296/.389/.457 with eight homers in 71 games in Single-A while generating huge exit velocities from both side of the plate. He's more athletic than most first basemen and may be able to handle the outfield corners.

Émilien Pitre, 2B, MetsThe best of the three prospects the Mets acquired from the Rays in the Freddy Peralta trade last month, Pitre excels at making contact and is batting .315/.430/.867 with a 10 percent strikeout rate in 107 games from High-A to Triple-A. He's not a slugger or a speedster, but he has some gap power and basestealing savvy.

Murf Gray, 3B, PiratesThe 73rd overall pick in the 2025 Draft -- making him the earliest Fresno State hitter selected since 2015 first-rounder Taylor Ward -- Gray has smashed expectations in his pro debut by slashing .304/.403/.575 with 31 homers in 115 games while climbing from Single-A to Double-A. He can get chase-happy but nevertheless makes a lot of contact, and his combination of bat speed and strength creates well-above-average raw power.

Cooper Flemming, SS, RaysFlemming rode some late helium into the second round of the 2025 Draft, pairing a clean left-handed swing with projectable power. In his age-19 season, the California prep product ranks second in the Single-A Carolina League in hitting (.293), fifth in wRC+ (124) and eighth in slugging (.443). He may wind up at third base, where his offensive profile and strong arm would fit well.

Eric Hartman, OF, BravesThe highest-ranked Top 100 prospect on this list at No. 42, Hartman is the first Minor Leaguer to accumulate 25 homers and 50 steals in the same season since Hall of Famer Andruw Jones in 1995. An over-slot 20th-round signing out of an Alberta high school two years ago, he has electrifying speed and is hitting balls a lot harder in his second pro season than he did in his debut.

Braylon Payne, OF, BrewersA surprise first-round pick out of a Texas high school in 2024, Payne stood out with his plus-plus speed at the time and since has developed surprising power. He may have the best combination of exit velocities and quickness in the Minors, and that has translated into 25 homers and 24 steals in 91 games between High-A and Double-A during his age-19 season.

Josiah Ragsdale, OF, CardinalsPart of the Dustin May/JoJo Romero trade with the Brewers in August, Ragsdale went from making a lot of weak groundball contact during his brief pro debut last year to driving balls in the air with authority this season. The 2025 seventh-rounder from Boston College also has plus-plus speed and is batting .305/.427/.563 with 23 homers and 34 steals in 106 games between High-A and Double-A.

Enddy Azocar, DH, OriolesAnother Venezuelan bargain ($40,000) for the Red Sox in their 2024 international class, Azocar went to the Orioles as part of the Adley Rutschman trade in August. He's a potential 20-20 right fielder with the chance for solid tools across the board, and he's hitting .299/.352/.549 with 21 homers and 18 steals in 106 games between two Class A levels at age 19.

Caden Hunter, LHP, OriolesThe Orioles have two lefties drafted in 2025 who made rapid ascents to the Top 100 list, with Hunter getting the nod over Joseph Dzierwa because he made the bigger jump. Selected in the sixth round out of Southern California, Hunter has dominated to the tune of a 2.01 ERA, .173 opponent average and 37 percent strikeout rate while advancing from Single-A to Double-A. He has added fastball velocity this year, now operating at 93-96 mph and reaching 99 with plenty of carry and armside run, and his mid-80s slider and changeup also are solid offerings.

Nolan Perry, RHP, Blue JaysAfter the Blue Jays drafted him in the 12th round out of a New Mexico high school in 2022, Perry blew out his elbow two years later and missed last season while recovering from Tommy John surgery. Now he's back with a better fastball than ever, averaging 94 mph with nice shape, and spinning solid sliders and curveballs. He has pitched well at three levels from Single-A to Double-A, compiling a 2.81 ERA, .196 opponent average and 35 percent K rate.

items.titleEn: Blue Jays recall Tiedemann, Keys as September reinforcements
items.summaryEn: Lefty reliever Mantiply, utility man Smith also activated
bodyEn: The Blue Jays announced they are returning left-handed pitcher Ricky Tiedemann and infielder Sean Keys to their Major League roster among five moves on Tuesday -- the day active rosters expanded to 28 players.

In addition to Tiedemann and Keys’ recalls, Toronto also reinstated left-handed pitcher Joe Mantiply from the 60-day injured list (left knee inflammation) and infielder Josh Smith from the 10-day IL (left hamstring inflammation). Both will be active for Tuesday’s series opener against the Guardians.

In a corresponding move, the Blue Jays designated outfielder Daz Cameron for assignment. The club also announced that right-handed pitcher Simeon Woods Richardson cleared outright waivers and elected free agency.

Tiedemann, currently the club’s No. 11 prospect according to MLB Pipeline, will make his second Major League appearance whenever he toes the rubber. Formerly the organization’s top overall prospect before a lengthy injury recovery, Tiedemann debuted on Aug. 15 and threw 1 2/3 innings against the Yankees, allowing one run while striking out two. The 24-year-old has posted a 3.75 ERA in 11 Minor League appearances this season.

Keys will similarly make his second trip to the Majors after a 12-game cup of coffee in June and July. The club’s No. 6 prospect, he leads Blue Jays Minor Leaguers with 28 home runs in 100 games. Keys, 23, hit one dinger and went 5-for-36 (.167) to start his big league career.
Acquired from the Rangers at the Trade Deadline, Smith played just 14 games for Toronto before going down with a hamstring injury. He was slashing .250/.323/.464 post-trade in a utility role.
Finally, Mantiply appeared in 17 games to begin the season, pitching to a 2.04 ERA before injury.

items.titleEn: Blue Jays have golden opportunity to tighten Wild Card race with Guardians
bodyEn: After a vintage Max Scherzer performance punctuated a three-game sweep of the Mariners this past weekend, the Blue Jays -- through all the adversity they’ve faced this season -- sit just 1 1/2 games back of the third American League Wild Card spot.
And they have a premium chance to close that gap this week.
The Blue Jays begin a three-game set against the Guardians -- the team currently holding that third Wild Card slot -- on Tuesday at Progressive Field.

It’s perhaps the biggest series of the season for Toronto to date, and the club has planned accordingly. Manager John Schneider used Monday’s off-day to make sure AL Cy Young contender Dylan Cease and José Soriano will pitch in the series on Wednesday and Thursday, respectively. Spencer Arrighetti is scheduled to throw on Tuesday, with Spencer Miles as an opener.

Across from that Toronto trio will be Cleveland’s Gavin Williams on Tuesday, Joey Cantillo on Wednesday and a to-be-announced starter on Thursday. Tuesday and Wednesday are night games with first pitch scheduled for 6:40 p.m. ET, while Thursday is a day game at 1:10 p.m. ET.
Here are three storylines to watch entering the series.
1. Tie it down

Beyond the straightforward importance of beating the team in front of you in the standings, the Blue Jays also enter with a 2-1 advantage over the Guardians in the season series. Clinching the season set would give Toronto the head-to-head tiebreaker over Cleveland, should it be necessary in determining playoff position.

Furthermore, the Blue Jays are in pole position entering September against four of the six teams which are primary threats to the final Wild Card spot. They are 2-1 against the Guardians with three games remaining; 4-3 against the Orioles with six games remaining; 4-2 against the Mariners with no games remaining; and 2-1 against the Tigers with three games remaining.
The Blue Jays only trail the Twins (3-4 with no remaining games) and the Rangers (0-4 with three games left).
If Toronto were to end the season tied with any of those teams for the final postseason berth, the head-to-head record would be the first tiebreaker, followed by intra-division record.
Swingin’ it
The Blue Jays’ 17-11 August -- their best month in 2026 -- was fueled not only by Cease’s continued excellence (2.03 ERA in five starts) but also by three key offensive performances.

Alejandro Kirk posted a 160 wRC+ -- a metric that measures overall offensive production on a 100-point scale -- that would make him the 14th-best hitter in MLB in August. George Springer finished the month at 25th with a 141 wRC+, while Trade Deadline addition Brett Bateman was 51st with a 127 wRC+.

After missing a large chunk of the season with a left thumb fracture, Kirk looked more like himself in August, hitting .341 with five home runs, 20 RBIs and more walks (12) than strikeouts (nine). The catcher was held hitless just three times in the 22 games he started, while he posted multiple hits seven times.

Springer shook off a slow start to the season and has been excellent in the second half. After going 7-for-11 with four extra-base hits in three games against the Mariners, the 36-year-old’s post-All-Star Game OPS is up to .892.

Meanwhile, Bateman -- after making his Major League debut on Aug. 7 -- has hit in 15 of his first 19 games. Acquired in the Kevin Gausman trade with the Cubs, the outfielder has taken over the Blue Jays’ leadoff spot and has reached base at a strong .384 mark.
Can he get going?

Vladimir Guerrero Jr.’s surprisingly down season has been well-documented, as he's still awaiting his first home run at Rogers Center since ... last season. He also hit one home run in August while slashing .221/.259/.312 -- good for just a 59 wRC+.

It’s clear that Guerrero has not been “right” all season, and he missed some time this past month with a concussion. But he has the support of his manager, and if Vladdy can put together even a mini hot streak in the season’s final month, it could do wonders for the Blue Jays’ final push toward October.

items.titleEn: Beloved 'Voice of the Expos' Doucet dies at 86
bodyEn: Jacques Doucet, known as the “Voice of the Expos”, died at 86 last week, his daughter Martine confirmed on social media. Doucet spent 33 years as the beloved French language play-by-play broadcaster for the Expos and served as a pivotal figure in popularizing the French vocabulary used to describe baseball.

A cause of death was not disclosed, but Doucet revealed in 2024 that he was battling Alzheimer’s disease. The Blue Jays honored him with a moment of silence before last Friday’s game against the Mariners.

“We join the MLB community and our colleagues at TVA Sports in extending our sincere condolences to the family and friends of Jacques Doucet,” the Blue Jays wrote in a statement. “The ‘Voice of Baseball’ in Quebec and a Canadian Baseball Hall of Famer - his impact on the game and the Montreal Expos will be remembered forever.”

Born in Montreal in 1940, Doucet got his start as a sports journalist with The Canadian Press and later covered the Expos' first years for La Presse. He became the club’s full-time French-language radio voice in 1972 and stayed in the role until the franchise left to become the Washington Nationals following the 2004 season.

Doucet then called independent league games for the Quebec Capitales, a member of the Can-Am League, from 2006 until 2011. An opportunity to return to the Major Leagues arose, and Doucet continued his career as the French broadcaster of Blue Jays games from 2011 until his retirement in 2022.

Among more than 5,500 MLB broadcasts, Doucet was on hand for the Expos’ 1981 NLCS run and two perfect games: Dennis Martinez in 1991, for the Expos against the Dodgers, and David Cone in 1999, for the Yankees against the Expos. He also provided French-language broadcasts for World Series games from 1982 through 1999.

Doucet additionally wrote several books, including “Les Secrets du baseball” with former Major League pitcher Claude Raymond and “Il était une fois les Expos,” a history of the franchise co-written with Marc Robitaille.

Doucet’s illustrious career featured an induction to the Expos’ Hall of Fame in 2003, the Quebec Baseball Hall of Fame in 2002 and the Canadian Baseball Hall of Fame in 2020. He also received the Canadian Baseball Hall of Fame’s Jack Graney Award in 2004 and was a finalist for the National Baseball Hall of Fame’s Ford C. Frick Award on multiple occasions.
items.titleZh: '博览会之声' Doucet 去世，享年86岁
items.summaryZh: '博览会之声' Doucet 去世，享年86岁，曾为博览会队和蓝鸟队担任法语解说。
bodyZh: 被誉为“博览会之声”的 Jacques Doucet 上周去世，享年86岁，他的女儿 Martine 在社交媒体上证实了这一消息。Doucet 曾担任博览会队深受喜爱的法语实况解说员长达33年，并在推广描述棒球的法语词汇方面发挥了关键作用。
死因尚未公布，但 Doucet 在2024年透露自己正在与阿尔茨海默病作斗争。蓝鸟队在上周五对阵水手队的比赛前为他默哀片刻。
蓝鸟队在一份声明中写道：“我们与 MLB 大家庭以及 TVA Sports 的同事们一起，向 Jacques Doucet 的家人和朋友致以诚挚的哀悼。他是魁北克的‘棒球之声’，也是加拿大棒球名人堂成员——他对这项运动和蒙特利尔博览会队的影响将被永远铭记。”
Doucet 于1940年出生于蒙特利尔，最初在加拿大通讯社担任体育记者，后来为《La Presse》报道了博览会队最初的几个赛季。1972年，他成为该俱乐部法语电台的专职解说员，直到2004赛季结束后球队迁往华盛顿成为华盛顿国民队。
此后，Doucet 于2006年至2011年担任独立联盟球队魁北克首都队（Can-Am 联盟成员）的比赛解说。后来出现了重返大联盟的机会，Doucet 于2011年起担任蓝鸟队比赛的法语解说，直至2022年退休。
在超过5500场 MLB 转播中，Doucet 参与了博览会队1981年国联冠军赛的征程，以及两场完全比赛：1991年 Dennis Martinez 代表博览会队对阵道奇队，以及1999年 David Cone 代表洋基队对阵博览会队。他还于1982年至1999年期间为世界大赛提供法语转播。
此外，Doucet 还写了几本书，包括与前大联盟投手 Claude Raymond 合著的《Les Secrets du baseball》，以及与 Marc Robitaille 合著的队史《Il était une fois les Expos》。
Doucet 辉煌的职业生涯包括2003年入选博览会队名人堂、2002年入选魁北克棒球名人堂以及2020年入选加拿大棒球名人堂。他还于2004年获得加拿大棒球名人堂的 Jack Graney 奖，并多次入围国家棒球名人堂的 Ford C. Frick 奖最终名单。

items.titleEn: Which franchise legend could be next to join Blue Jays' Hall of Excellence?
bodyEn: TORONTO -- Across the many renovations that have modernized Rogers Centre, some of the most important changes the Blue Jays have made look to the past.

First came the nods to history along the 100 level, where the pillars now hold displays with memorabilia from 50 seasons of Blue Jays baseball. Then came the back-to-back World Series statue in front of the stadium, that famous image of Joe Carter. This past weekend brought the main attraction, though, when the Blue Jays opened their Hall of Excellence and inducted the great Buck Martinez, who joined the 11 existing members.

Five years ago, the Blue Jays had the Level of Excellence wrapped around the facing of the 400 level, but the club’s history wasn’t accessible enough. Young fans, or even fans in their 20s and 30s, weren’t hearing the stories of Dave Stieb, George Bell and those great teams of the 1980s often enough. That’s changed.

“The Hall of Excellence creates a permanent home for the stories, achievement and memories of the players and leaders who helped build this franchise and shape Blue Jays history,” said club president and CEO Mark Shapiro at the unveiling. “The individuals represented here established the foundation of this organization and we are proud to ensure that their stories will continue to be told for years to come.”

This also included a call for fans to be part of the process moving forward, with voting now open on the club’s website. Along with a write-in option, the names suggested are: Devon White, Edwin Encarnación, Ernie Whitt, Fred McGriff, Tom Henke, Jimmy Key, John Olerud, Pat Hentgen, Lloyd Moseby, Jesse Barfield, Vernon Wells, Juan Guzmán, Jim Clancy and Duane Ward.
With a clear intent to grow this space, it begs the question: Who’s next?
LHP Jimmy Key (1984-1992)
When you get past franchise icons Stieb and Roy Halladay, who will share the tops of these franchise leaderboards forever, you start running into Key’s name an awful lot.

His 3.42 ERA with the Blue Jays is tied with Stieb -- and just 0.01 runs better than Halladay -- over 1,695 2/3 innings. Key and Stieb led so many of those great rotations through the mid- and late 80s, Key the lefty who was always under control, Stieb the fiery right-hander. Beyond Stieb and Halladay, only Clancy has thrown more innings in a Blue Jays uniform than Key.
RHP Tom Henke (1985-1992)

The greatest closer in Blue Jays history, Henke and the late Ward formed a back end that feels decades ahead of its time in hindsight. Henke’s 217 saves tower above the rest, with Ward’s 121 the closest in second place.

Henke’s case runs up against what so many others do, which is that we’re talking about tenures of six or eight years, not 10 or 12, which could be the tipping point. The importance of Henke’s addition prior to the 1985 season can never be overstated, though, and the role he played in taking the young Blue Jays organization to another level must always be remembered.
DH Edwin Encarnación (2009-2016)

Once again, if Encarnación had played a few more seasons in Toronto, this case would be undeniable. His run from 2012-16 was remarkable, though, forming one of the most feared one-two punches in baseball alongside José Bautista.

Encarnación works as an interesting debate alongside Vernon Wells and Josh Donaldson, and there’s no wrong answer here. Do you prefer a player who was truly elite in a short time like Donaldson, a player who was very good over the medium term like Encarnación, or a player who was solid for parts of 12 seasons in Toronto and climbed plenty of all-time leaderboards like Wells?
Broadcaster Jerry Howarth
The radio voice of the Blue Jays for 36 seasons, Howarth brought us so much of this organization’s history right alongside Tom Cheek, who he could someday join again in the Hall of Excellence.

Martinez was recently inducted under the “Builders and Broadcasters” designation, which also applies to Cheek, Paul Beeston and Pat Gillick. The Blue Jays have a rich media history that stretches into the press box, including the Hall of Famer Bob Elliott and Alison Gordon, who in 1979 became the first woman to cover an MLB beat full-time for the Toronto Star.

Broadcasters welcome fans into the game every night, though, like Dan Shulman and Joe Siddall do now. For 36 years, Blue Jays fans turned on their radio and heard that familiar voice of Howarth welcoming them … “Hello, friends!”
items.titleZh: 下一位加入蓝鸟卓越名人堂的球队传奇是谁？
items.summaryZh: 蓝鸟卓越名人堂候选名单公布，谁将是下一位入选的传奇？
bodyZh: 多伦多——在让 Rogers Centre 现代化的多次翻新中，蓝鸟队所做的一些最重要改变却着眼于过去。
首先是在100层看台对历史的致敬，那里的柱子上现在陈列着蓝鸟队50个赛季的纪念品。然后是体育场前的背靠背世界大赛雕像，那是 Joe Carter 的著名形象。不过，上周末迎来了重头戏，蓝鸟队开启了他们的卓越名人堂，并入选了伟大的 Buck Martinez，他加入了现有的11位成员。
五年前，蓝鸟队的“卓越层”环绕在400层看台的正面，但球队的历史还不够亲近。年轻球迷，甚至二十多岁和三十多岁的球迷，并不经常听到 Dave Stieb、George Bell 以及那些1980年代伟大球队的故事。如今这已经改变。
俱乐部主席兼首席执行官 Mark Shapiro 在揭幕仪式上表示：“卓越名人堂为那些帮助建立这支球队、塑造蓝鸟历史的球员和领袖的故事、成就和回忆提供了一个永久的家。这里所代表的个人奠定了这支球队的基础，我们很自豪能够确保他们的故事在未来多年继续被讲述。”

这还包括呼吁球迷参与未来的评选过程，俱乐部网站上的投票现已开放。除了手写选项外，建议的名字还有：Devon White、Edwin Encarnación、Ernie Whitt、Fred McGriff、Tom Henke、Jimmy Key、John Olerud、Pat Hentgen、Lloyd Moseby、Jesse Barfield、Vernon Wells、Juan Guzmán、Jim Clancy 和 Duane Ward。
怀着明确扩展这一空间的意图，问题随之而来：下一位是谁？
左投手 Jimmy Key（1984-1992）
当你越过球队偶像 Stieb 和 Roy Halladay——他们将永远占据球队历史榜单的顶端——你会开始频繁看到 Key 的名字。
他在蓝鸟队的自责分率为3.42，与 Stieb 持平，比 Halladay 低0.01分，投了1695又2/3局。Key 和 Stieb 在80年代中后期领衔了众多伟大的先发轮值，Key 是永远掌控局面的左投手，Stieb 是火热的右投手。在 Stieb 和 Halladay 之外，只有 Clancy 身披蓝鸟战袍的投球局数超过 Key。
右投手 Tom Henke（1985-1992）
作为蓝鸟队历史上最伟大的终结者，Henke 与已故的 Ward 组成的后援组合，事后看来领先于那个时代数十年。Henke 的217次救援成功高居队史之首，Ward 的121次紧随其后位列第二。
Henke 的案例与许多其他人一样，我们谈论的是六或八年的任期，而不是十年或十二年，这可能是决定性因素。然而，Henke 在1985赛季前加盟的重要性怎么强调都不为过，他在将年轻的蓝鸟队提升到另一个层次中所扮演的角色必须永远被铭记。
指定打击 Edwin Encarnación（2009-2016）
再一次，如果 Encarnación 在多伦多多打几个赛季，他的入选将无可争议。不过，他在2012-16赛季的表现非常出色，与 José Bautista 组成了棒球界最令人生畏的双人组合之一。
Encarnación 与 Vernon Wells 和 Josh Donaldson 构成了一个有趣的辩论，这里没有错误答案。你更喜欢像 Donaldson 那样在短时间内真正精英的球员，像 Encarnación 那样在中期内表现出色的球员，还是像 Wells 那样在多伦多效力12个赛季且在大量历史榜单中攀升的稳健球员？
解说员 Jerry Howarth
作为蓝鸟队36个赛季的电台之声，Howarth 与 Tom Cheek 一起为我们带来了这支球队的众多历史，他或许有一天能再次在卓越名人堂中与 Cheek 相聚。
Martinez 最近以“建设者与解说员”的身份入选，这一类别也适用于 Cheek、Paul Beeston 和 Pat Gillick。蓝鸟队有着丰富的媒体历史，延伸到记者席，包括名人堂成员 Bob Elliott 和 Alison Gordon，后者在1979年成为首位全职为《多伦多星报》报道 MLB 球队的女性。
不过，解说员每晚都欢迎球迷进入比赛，就像现在 Dan Shulman 和 Joe Siddall 所做的那样。36年来，蓝鸟球迷打开收音机，听到 Howarth 那熟悉的声音欢迎他们……“朋友们，你们好！”

items.titleEn: Mad Max makes more history, strikes out 10 to pass Perry for 9th all-time
bodyEn: TORONTO -- Max Scherzer climbed another rung of the all-time Major League Baseball strikeouts ladder in the Blue Jays’ 7-0 win over the Mariners on Sunday.
With his seventh-inning punch out of Cal Raleigh, his 10th of the game, Scherzer surpassed Gaylord Perry for ninth all-time with 3,535 strikeouts.
When it was announced to the Rogers Centre crowd, fans erupted in appreciation for the history they were witnessing. In typical Scherzer fashion, he saluted the crowd before getting back to work.

It was the 115th time in Scherzer’s illustrious career that he had struck out at least 10 batters in a game. He is third in that category, behind only Nolan Ryan (215) and Randy Johnson (212) since the mound moved to its current distance in 1893.
Every member of the 3,000-strikeout club

At 42 years and 34 days old, Scherzer is also the oldest pitcher with 10+ strikeouts and one or no hits allowed in a game since Ryan on May 1, 1991, (44 years, 90 days) in a no-hitter against none other than the Blue Jays.
Scherzer and Ryan (six times) are the only pitchers with such an outing at age 42+ in MLB history.

After Josh Naylor grounded out to second base to end the seventh, Scherzer walked off the mound with a 4-0 lead and a standing ovation from the Jays faithful. Scherzer threw 67 of his 97 pitches for strikes, with one walk and Raleigh's fourth-inning double the only baserunners he allowed.
items.titleZh: Mad Max再创历史，单场10K超越Perry升至历史第9位
items.summaryZh: Scherzer单场10次三振，生涯3535K超越Perry，升至历史第9位。
bodyZh: 多伦多——Max Scherzer在周日蓝鸟7-0战胜水手的比赛中，在大联盟历史三振榜上又登上了一级台阶。
凭借第七局对Cal Raleigh投出的三振，也是本场比赛的第10次三振，Scherzer以3535次三振超越Gaylord Perry，升至历史第九位。
当这一消息在罗杰斯中心球场宣布时，现场球迷爆发出欢呼，感谢他们正在见证历史。Scherzer以他一贯的方式向人群致意，然后重新投入比赛。
这是Scherzer辉煌职业生涯中第115次在单场比赛中三振至少10名打者。自1893年投手丘移到目前距离以来，他在这项数据上排名第三，仅次于Nolan Ryan（215次）和Randy Johnson（212次）。
3000次三振俱乐部的每一位成员
在42岁零34天的时候，Scherzer也成为自1991年5月1日Ryan在对阵蓝鸟的比赛中投出无安打（44岁零90天）以来，单场三振10次以上且最多只被击出一支安打的年龄最大的投手。
在大联盟历史上，Scherzer和Ryan（6次）是仅有的在42岁及以上还曾做到单场10K且最多被打1安的投手。
当Josh Naylor在第七局击出二垒方向滚地球出局后，Scherzer带着4-0的领先优势走下投手丘，全场蓝鸟球迷起立鼓掌。Scherzer共投97球，其中67球为好球，仅投出一次保送，另有Raleigh在第四局击出的二垒安打，这是对手仅有的两次上垒。

items.titleEn: Jays' top pitching prospect helps Double-A squad to latest bit of delicious history
bodyEn: Unique happenings are often afoot when the Double-A New Hampshire Fisher Cats dip into their alternate identity bag and step out as the Manchester Chicken Tenders.

On June 7, 2025, Rafael Sanchez spun a seven-inning no-hitter when the team took the field as the Buffalo Tenders, a spicy offshoot. Incredibly, they were back at it again April 28 when four Fisher Cats hurlers combined to toss yet another no-no while under the guise of the Chicken Tenders.

So when Nolan Perry, the Blue Jays’ No. 2 prospect, toed the slab Saturday night, it was a precursor that something special could happen. Add in that it was the second time ever the club was donning their latest offshoot -- the Coconut Tenders -- and it all came together for a perfectly delicious blend of history during the club’s 6-4 loss to Hartford at Delta Dental Stadium.
Get tickets to a Minor League game near you »

Perry lost the no-hit bid right out of the chute, so the Tenders would have to find an even sweeter way to make history. The 2026 All-Star Futures Game representative racked up a pair of strikeouts in both the first and second, then notched a fifth in the third, before adding two more in the fourth, marking his eighth start this season with at least seven punchouts to his credit.

But when the bullpen door swung open, batters kept on swinging and missing. Righty Alex Amalfi notched five strikeouts in two frames. Gage Stanifer (TOR No. 10) notched all six of his outs by way of the K before Yondrei Rojas added two punchouts of his own. All told, the Fisher Cats’ pitching staff finished with 20 strikeouts, the most in franchise history.

Perry topped out at 75 pitches as Toronto continues to keep a close eye on his workload in his first season back from Tommy John surgery. He’s already up to a career-high 73 2/3 innings this year and missed a chunk of time after taking a line drive off the head. But when healthy, he’s backed up being ranked No. 95 overall by MLB Pipeline with a 2.81 ERA, .196 average against and 12.6 K/9 across three levels.

Stanifer first pitched out of relief this season back on Aug. 6 and has since made seven appearances as a multi-inning reliever. He’s racked up 22 strikeouts over 14 innings in that span and held opposing batters to a .184 average. Equipped with one of the most wicked one-two punches of offerings in the Jays’ system with his fastball/slider combo, Stanifer has shown an ability to continue missing bats in his new role.

The addition of the Coconut Tenders to the alt identity family was meant to bring a bit of sweet summer vibes to the Granite State. But it’s also provided the Fisher Cats with a little extra flavor as they make history.
items.titleZh: 蓝鸟顶级投手新秀助2A球队再创美味历史
items.summaryZh: 蓝鸟潜力新秀助2A球队单场20次三振创队史纪录
bodyZh: 当2A新罕布什尔费舍猫队（New Hampshire Fisher Cats）从他们的替补身份包中拿出另一个身份，以曼彻斯特鸡柳队（Manchester Chicken Tenders）出场时，独特的事情往往会发生。
2025年6月7日，Rafael Sanchez 在球队以“布法罗鸡柳”这个香辣分支身份出战时就投出了一场七局无安打比赛。不可思议的是，4月28日他们又做到了——四位费舍猫投手在“鸡柳”身份下联手投出了另一场无安打比赛。
因此，当蓝鸟队2号潜力新秀Nolan Perry周六晚上踏上投手丘时，这预示着可能会发生一些特别的事情。再加上这是球队第二次穿上最新分支身份“椰子鸡柳”（Coconut Tenders），这一切汇聚成了一段完美而美味的历史，尽管球队在Delta Dental球场以6比4输给了Hartford。
购买附近小联盟比赛门票 »
Perry 一开始就失去了无安打比赛的希望，因此鸡柳队需要找到一种更甜蜜的方式来创造历史。这位2026年全明星未来之星赛代表在第一局和第二局各投出两次三振，第三局又添一次，第四局再添两次，这是他本赛季第八次先发至少投出七次三振。
但当牛棚门打开后，打者们继续挥棒落空。右投手Alex Amalfi在两局中投出五次三振。Gage Stanifer（蓝鸟第10号新秀）用三振解决了他所有六个出局数，随后Yondrei Rojas也贡献了两次三振。总的来说，费舍猫队投手群合计送出20次三振，创下队史纪录。
Perry 最多投了75球，多伦多方面在他从汤米·约翰手术复出的首个赛季中继续密切关注他的工作量。他的投球局数今年已经达到职业生涯最高的73又2/3局，并且曾因头部被平飞球击中而缺阵过一段时间。但健康时，他在三个级别中展现出了与MLB Pipeline将他排在第95位相符的实力——自责分率2.81，对手打击率.196，每九局三振12.6次。
Stanifer 本赛季首次以后援身份出场是在8月6日，此后他已七次作为多局后援投手上场。在这段时间里，他在14局中投出22次三振，并将对手打击率限制在.184。凭借他的速球/滑球组合，这被认为是蓝鸟系统中最犀利的组合拳之一，Stanifer在新角色中展现出了持续让打者挥空的能力。
将“椰子鸡柳”加入替补身份家族，是为了给花岗岩州带来一丝甜蜜的夏日气息。但这也为费舍猫队创造历史增添了一点别样的风味。
